title: Institutional confidence remains near historic lows while technology and small-business legitimacy diverge
source_unit: Gallup annual Confidence in Institutions poll and long-running institution trend series

observations.period: June 1-15, 2026; average confidence in 14 core institutions

denominator.unit: average percentage expressing a great deal or quite a lot of confidence across 14 Gallup-tracked institutions

average_confidence.unit: percent average confidence; one point above the 2023 record low

years_below_30.unit: consecutive years with average confidence below 30%

observations.method: Gallup institution-specific confidence survey; aggregate is an arithmetic average across the 14 institutions, not a respondent-level confidence index.
observations.uncertainty: Institutions have different histories, salience, response distributions, and political meaning. An average can conceal high confidence in one institution and very low confidence in another; it does not measure behavior or performance directly.
observations.subgroup: US adults across 14 public and private institutions; party differences are reported separately.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low average confidence does not imply generalized withdrawal; crisis, presidential control, affordability concerns, and institution-specific events can move ratings differently.

denominator.unit: percent of US adults rating each institution; institution-specific survey items

large_technology_companies.unit: percent expressing a great deal or quite a lot of confidence

small_business.unit: percent expressing a great deal or quite a lot of confidence

observations.method: Gallup institution-specific estimates; large technology companies and small business are not interchangeable firm-sector categories.
observations.uncertainty: The contrast does not identify local experience, employment, prices, innovation, political power, data practices, news coverage, or consumer switching.
observations.subgroup: US adults rating large technology companies and small business; no subgroup decomposition in this observation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low confidence in large technology companies can coexist with high use and dependence; high small-business confidence does not imply universal access or fairness.

observations.period: June 1-15, 2026; partisan difference in average institutional confidence

denominator.unit: percent within Republican and Democratic party-identification groups across Gallup's long-running institution list

republican_minus_democratic_confidence.unit: percentage-point average confidence gap, Republicans higher than Democrats

presidency_gap.unit: percentage-point Republican-over-Democratic confidence contrast for the presidency

observations.method: Gallup party-conditioned institution comparisons; the source reports institution-specific contrasts and a long-running average gap.
observations.uncertainty: Party confidence differences can reflect who holds political power, identity, institutional judgments, and response styles; they are not causal estimates of polarization or evidence of party-wide behavior.
observations.subgroup: Republicans and Democrats in the Gallup poll; partisan identification is not treated as a fixed mechanism.
observations.counterinterpretation: Partisan confidence can rise in institutions associated with one's governing coalition without translating into trust of all institutions, compliance, voting, or collective action.

related_sources.claim: Gallup's institution-confidence trend page defines the long-running series and institution list.
Pew's current press-government legitimacy layer provides a more specific information-institution comparison.

boundary: This record measures reported confidence in institutions, not institutional performance, legitimacy, usage, compliance, switching, political action, or causal polarization. The 14-institution average mixes public and private entities and must not replace institution-specific analysis.
